### Describe the Bug

When `_some` (or `_none`) on an o2m field has an `_and` / `_or` inside it, or more than one field, the filter gets dropped and every row comes back. No error, nothing in the logs. `_some` with a single field works fine.

Leaving `_some` out and putting the `_and` straight on the o2m field does work, and all conditions are checked against the same related item, so that's my workaround for now. `_none` has no equivalent though, so "no related item where A and B" can't be expressed at all right now.

We noticed because a "currently enrolled" filter on our students (`enrollment: { _some: { _and: [start <= now, end null or >= now] } }`) was returning every student, 51 instead of 32.

Might be related to #25403 / #27704, but that's about `_some` further down the tree. Here it's directly on a top level o2m alias, and nothing gets rejected, it's just silently ignored.

### To Reproduce

Clean container, sqlite. `parent` has an o2m alias `children`, `child` has `label` (string), `n` (integer) and `parent` (m2o).

- P1: child (a, 1)
- P2: children (a, 2) and (b, 1)
- P3: child (c, 3)

`GET /items/parent?fields=name&filter=...`:

```
filter                                                          expected   got
children: { _some: { label: { _eq: "a" } } }                    P1 P2      P1 P2
children: { _some: { _and: [{ label: { _eq: "a" } }] } }        P1 P2      P1 P2 P3
children: { _some: { label: { _eq: "a" }, n: { _eq: 1 } } }     P1         P1 P2 P3
children: { _some: { _and: [{ label: a }, { n: 1 }] } }         P1         P1 P2 P3
children: { _none: { _and: [{ label: a }, { n: 1 }] } }         P2 P3      P1 P2 P3
children: { _and: [{ label: a }, { n: 1 }] }   (no _some)       P1         P1
```

Same results on 11.17.4 and 12.4.1. Originally hit it on Postgres.

### Describe the Bug

When a project has enough collections for the module navigation to scroll, the navigation jumps back to the top on almost every navigation. If you scroll down to reach a collection near the bottom of the list, open it, and then want to go to a neighbouring collection, the list has already scrolled back to the top and you have to scroll down again.

The module navigation's scroll container lives inside `PrivateView`, which each route component mounts itself (`app/src/modules/content/routes/collection.vue`, `item.vue`, …). Any navigation that swaps the route component therefore destroys the scroll container and creates a new one at `scrollTop: 0`, and nothing persists the offset.

That means the reset happens on every navigation between different route records, not just within Content:

| Navigation | Nav scroll offset |
| --- | --- |
| collection list → another collection list (same route record) | preserved |
| collection list → item detail | **reset to 0** |
| item detail → another collection | **reset to 0** |
| Content → Settings → Content | **reset to 0** |

### To Reproduce

1. Create enough collections that the module navigation scrolls (25 collections at a 1440×640 viewport is enough).
2. Go to **Content** and open the first collection.
3. Scroll the module navigation to the bottom.
4. Open any item in the collection (or click a collection while an item detail page is open).
5. The module navigation is back at the top.

Measured with Playwright against `directus/directus:12.3.1`, reading `#module-navigation` `scrollTop` before and after each navigation:

```
  OK   | collection list -> other collection: 310 -> 310
 RESET | item detail -> other collection: 310 -> 0
 RESET | collection list -> item detail (row click): 310 -> 0
 RESET | module switch: content -> settings -> content: 310 -> 0
  OK   | browser back after navigating away: 310 -> 310
```

### Directus Version

v12.3.1

Self-Hosted (Docker Image)

SQLite 3

### Describe the Bug

On Oracle, a field created with type `time` does not survive the schema round-trip — it comes back as `timestamp`. Every code path that branches on the field type then treats `"10:15:30"` as a timestamp, so reading, writing and filtering a time field all break.

**1. The column is created as a timestamp.** Oracle has no `TIME` type. [`addColumnToTable`](https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/main/api/src/services/fields.ts#L952-L953) falls through to `table[field.type](field.field)`, and knex's oracledb dialect maps `.time()` to `timestamp with local time zone`:

```
COLUMN_NAME: 'tm', DATA_TYPE: 'TIMESTAMP(6) WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE'
```

**2. Nothing records that it was meant to be a time.** `DateHelperOracle.fieldFlagForField` only returns a `cast-*` special for `json` and `dateTime`; there is no `cast-time`, so `special` stays `null`.

**3. So the field reads back as `timestamp`.** `getLocalType` does `data_type.toLowerCase().split('(')[0]` → `"timestamp"` → `'timestamp'`.

**4. `PayloadService.processDates` then parses the time string as a timestamp.** The `read` branch does `new Date("10:15:30").toISOString()`, which throws `RangeError: Invalid time value`. This fires from `prepareDelta` while building the revision delta, so the request 500s before the insert is even attempted.

Two further consequences:

- **The write path would corrupt silently rather than fail.** The `timestamp` write branch calls `writeTimestamp` → `parseISO("10:15:30")` → `Invalid Date`, with **no `isValid` guard** — unlike the `date` and `dateTime` branches immediately above it, which throw `InvalidPayloadError`. Binding an `Invalid Date` to Oracle does not error; it stores garbage. A direct knex insert of `Invalid Date` into the column above stored `-004713-01-28T16:19:15.000Z`. This missing guard is not Oracle-specific and is worth fixing on its own.
- **Filtering on a time value fails for a separate reason.** `DateHelperOracle.parse` only short-circuits strings that are ≤10 chars *and* contain `-`. `"10:15:30"` misses that and falls through to `new Date(date).toISOString()`, throwing the same `RangeError`.

There is an existing workaround for this in the e2e suite — `tests/e2e/tests/fields/timezone/timezone.sb.test.ts` strips `time` from the payload and skips the assertion when the database is Oracle.

### To Reproduce

Against a Directus instance backed by Oracle (reproduced on `gvenzl/oracle-free:23-slim-faststart`):

1. Create a collection with a `time` field:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"collection":"repro_time","schema":{},"meta":{},"fields":[
        {"field":"id","type":"integer","schema":{"is_primary_key":true,"has_auto_increment":true},"meta":{"hidden":true}},
        {"field":"tm","type":"time","schema":{},"meta":{}}]}' \
  "$URL/collections"
```

2. Read the field back — note `"type": "timestamp"`, not `"time"`:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$URL/fields/repro_time/tm"
```

```json
{ "type": "timestamp", "schema": { "data_type": "TIMESTAMP(6) WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE" } }
```

3. Insert a time value:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tm":"10:15:30"}' "$URL/items/repro_time"
```

**Expected:** the item is created and `tm` reads back as `"10:15:30"`.

**Actual:** `500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR`

```
RangeError: Invalid time value
    at Date.toISOString (<anonymous>)
    at PayloadService.processDates (api/dist/services/payload.js:267)
    at PayloadService.processValues
    at PayloadService.prepareDelta
    at api/dist/services/items.js:191
```

4. Filtering on a time value fails independently, with a different stack:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$URL/items/repro_time?filter\[tm\][_eq]=10:15:30"
```

```
RangeError: Invalid time value
    at Date.toISOString (<anonymous>)
    at DateHelperOracle.parse (api/dist/database/helpers/date/dialects/oracle.js:9:32)
    at applyOperator (api/dist/database/run-ast/lib/apply-query/filter/operator.js:106)
    at addWhereClauses
    at applyFilter
```

All four steps reproduce on every other supported database without error.

### Suggested fix

Make the round-trip lossless: have `DateHelperOracle.fieldFlagForField` return a `cast-time` flag for `time`, and have `getLocalType` honor it, following the existing `cast-datetime` / `cast-timestamp` pattern. The field then stays `type: 'time'`, `processDates` skips it in `dateColumns`, and the existing `timeColumns` read path formats it back as `HH:mm:ss`. The column still needs to hold the value sensibly — storing it against a fixed epoch date is the usual approach — and `DateHelperOracle.parse` needs a guard for time-shaped strings so filters work.

Separately, the `timestamp` write branch in `processDates` should get the same `isValid` check the `date` and `dateTime` branches have, so an unparseable value raises `InvalidPayloadError` instead of being written as an `Invalid Date`.

### Directus Version

main (`directus@12.3.1`, `@directus/api@39.1.0`)

### Hosting Strategy

Self-Hosted (Custom)

### Database

Oracle Database 23ai Free (`gvenzl/oracle-free:23-slim-faststart`)

### Describe the Bug

Dotted dynamic variable paths backed by arrays drop valid falsy values while resolving the path. Values such as `0`, `false`, and an empty string are removed, even though the property exists.

The shared `get` helper currently filters nested array results by truthiness. `parseDynamicVariable` uses that helper for dotted `$CURRENT_USER`, `$CURRENT_ROLES`, `$CURRENT_ROLE`, and `$CURRENT_POLICIES` paths, so permission filters, validation rules, and presets can receive a shorter list than the one represented by the configured data.

Only null, undefined, and missing properties should be excluded. Keeping null out is intentional because a null operand in a SQL `NOT IN` list can make the comparison unknown for every row.

This was reviewed with the Directus maintainers and confirmed as a normal correctness issue: https://github.com/directus/directus/security/advisories/GHSA-xgww-wpqg-cx4p#event-1035897

### To Reproduce

1. Resolve a dotted array-backed variable with data equivalent to:

   ```ts
   {
     $CURRENT_ROLES: [
       { value: 'blocked' },
       { value: 0 },
       { value: false },
       { value: '' },
       { value: null },
       { value: undefined },
       {},
     ],
   }
   ```

2. Use `$CURRENT_ROLES.value` as the operand of an `_in` or `_nin` filter.
3. Observe that the resolved list contains only `['blocked']`.
4. The expected list is `['blocked', 0, false, '']`. Null, undefined, and the missing property should remain excluded.

The same behavior can be reproduced directly with `get(context, '$CURRENT_ROLES.value', null)` from `@directus/utils`.

### Directus Version

v12.3.1 and `main` at `99ebe62`

### Hosting Strategy

Self-Hosted (Custom)

### Database

Database-independent. The values are lost during shared filter parsing before SQL generation.

### Describe the Bug

### Summary

Upgrading to Directus 12 removes a previously working capability: an instance configured against a **user-supplied, self-hosted LLM endpoint** (Ollama / vLLM / LiteLLM / any OpenAI-compatible base URL) loses that connection once license enforcement kicks in.

Per the [v12.0.0 release notes](https://github.com/directus/directus/releases/tag/v12.0.0), Core-tier self-hosted instances lose:

- **Custom or self-hosted LLMs — connections to custom LLMs will no longer work**
- AI Translations
- SSO
- Custom permission rules

Enforcement is immediate on new instances; upgraded instances get a 30-day grace period.

### Why this one is different from the others

The other gated features have a plausible "this is commercial functionality" story. This one inverts its own purpose: it takes the **cheapest, most privacy-preserving, most self-reliant** AI configuration and makes it the paid one, while the vendor-routed default presumably stays available.

There is also no vendor cost being recovered here. Blocking a user-supplied base URL and API key is not withholding a service Directus provides — it is an artificial restriction on where a self-hoster may point their own configuration.

### Who this breaks

- **Air-gapped / on-prem deployments.** No egress to a hosted model provider means no AI path at all. Not degraded — none.
- **Data-residency and GDPR-constrained setups.** Organizations running a local model precisely because they cannot send content to a third-party API are pushed to a commercial license or off Directus AI entirely.
- **Cost-controlled deployments.** Running your own inference on your own hardware was the main reason many self-hosters enabled these features.
- **The "free under $5M revenue / 50 employees" promise.** A qualifying team that self-hosts a model is effectively told their own inference endpoint is a paid feature.

### Expected behavior

A custom / self-hosted LLM endpoint configured by the operator should keep working on the Core tier, or at minimum under the free OIG license key.

### Suggested resolutions

1. Move **custom LLM endpoints** to Core and keep the gate on *Directus-provided* AI services (hosted inference, AI translations).
2. Keep the gate, but scope it to the vendor-routed path only — a user-configured base URL + key is not a Directus-delivered feature.
3. At minimum, enable custom LLM connections under the free OIG license so under-$5M teams are not excluded.

### Questions

- Was the intent to gate *Directus-hosted* inference, with custom endpoints caught in the same flag?
- Does the free OIG license key enable custom LLM connections, or is this Enterprise-only?
- Is there a supported way to keep a bring-your-own-model setup working on v12 without a paid license?

### To Reproduce

1. On Directus 11.x (self-hosted, no license key), configure a custom / self-hosted LLM provider — e.g. an OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as Ollama or vLLM with a custom base URL.
2. Confirm the AI features using that provider work (e.g. AI-assisted fields / translations / the MCP chat tooling backed by that endpoint).
3. Upgrade the instance to v12.x (e.g. `directus/directus:12.3.1`) without adding a license key.
4. Wait out the 30-day grace period, or start a fresh v12 instance where enforcement is immediate.
5. Trigger the same AI feature.

**Expected:** the request is sent to the configured self-hosted endpoint, as it was on v11.

**Actual:** the connection to the custom LLM is refused by license enforcement. Because the endpoint is self-hosted and possibly on an isolated network, there is no fallback provider available — the feature is simply gone.

_Note: filed here because the issue chooser routes feature requests to roadmap.directus.com and questions to community.directus.com. This is a behavioural regression between v11 and v12, so the bug form seemed the closest fit — happy to move it if there's a better venue._

### Directus Version

v12.3.1

### Hosting Strategy

Self-Hosted (Docker Image)

### Database

_No response_

### Describe the bug

`enforce_tfa` is currently resolved through two different mechanisms.

During `AuthenticationService.login()`, Directus checks for `enforce_tfa` with a bespoke query that only considers policies attached directly to the user's primary role. It does not include policies assigned directly to the user, policies inherited through parent roles, or `ip_access` filtering.

This differs from the normal `fetchPolicies()` behavior, which resolves policies from the user's complete role hierarchy and direct-user assignments, and applies `ip_access`. These behaviors are also covered by Directus' own tests.

`/policies/me/globals` uses this full effective-policy resolution when determining `enforce_tfa`.

This means a user can have different `enforce_tfa` state depending on the code path. For example, with an enforcing policy on a parent role:

```text
POST /auth/login JWT       → enforce_tfa absent
GET /policies/me/globals   → enforce_tfa true
```

This is relevant beyond JWT metadata: the OAuth2 and OpenID callback handlers explicitly inspect the JWT `enforce_tfa` claim to decide whether to redirect the user to `/admin/tfa-setup`.

There are two related inconsistencies:

* The login-side query ignores `ip_access`, so it can also return `enforce_tfa: true` for a policy that isn't effective for the current IP.
* `AuthenticationService.refresh()` creates a new JWT without recalculating or preserving `enforce_tfa`, so the claim disappears after refresh.

Data Studio itself mostly masks the first discrepancy because it hydrates `/policies/me/globals` and uses that value to redirect users without a `tfa_secret` to the TFA setup flow.

It seems preferable for login, refresh, SSO callbacks, and `/policies/me/globals` to use the same effective-policy semantics.

### To Reproduce

1. Create a policy with **Enforce TFA** enabled.

2. Create a role hierarchy:

   ```text
   Parent
   └── Child
   ```

3. Assign the policy to `Parent`.

4. Assign an active local user without configured TFA (`tfa_secret = null`) to `Child`.

5. Log in through `POST /auth/login`.

6. Decode the returned access token.

   **Actual:** `enforce_tfa` is absent.

7. Using the same access token, request:

   ```http
   GET /policies/me/globals
   ```

   **Actual:**

   ```json
   {
     "data": {
       "enforce_tfa": true
     }
   }
   ```

8. As a control, move the policy from `Parent` to the user's primary `Child` role and log in again.

   **Actual:** the initial JWT now contains `enforce_tfa: true`.

9. Refresh that session through `POST /auth/refresh` and decode the new access token.

   **Actual:** `enforce_tfa` is absent again, while `/policies/me/globals` still reports `true`.

The same login-vs-effective-policy mismatch can also be reproduced by assigning the enforcing policy directly to the user, or by using a primary-role policy with an `ip_access` restriction that does not match the request IP.


### Directus Version

12.2.0

### Hosting Strategy

image pixel dimensions. Meanwhile the asset pipeline *is* bounded by dimensions, via
`ASSETS_TRANSFORM_IMAGE_MAX_DIMENSION` and
`ASSETS_TRANSFORM_IMAGE_MAX_OUTPUT_DIMENSION`.

That asymmetry means an instance can accept an image it is then structurally unable
to serve a transform of. I would like an env var, e.g.
`FILES_MAX_UPLOAD_IMAGE_DIMENSION`, that rejects an upload whose width or height
exceeds it, returning a 4xx the same way `FILES_MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE` returns 413.

An optional companion `FILES_UPLOAD_IMAGE_RESIZE_MODE=reject|downscale` would let
operators downscale to the limit instead of rejecting, which is friendlier to
non-technical editors.

## Why bytes are not a usable proxy today

`FILES_MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE` is the closest existing control, but filesize and pixel
dimensions correlate poorly for the images that cause trouble. A real example from
our media library: a 9178x2470 PNG that is only ~300KB. It passes any sane byte
limit, and is then unusable for `format`/`quality` transforms.

## Concrete failure this produces

With `ASSETS_TRANSFORM_IMAGE_MAX_OUTPUT_DIMENSION=6000` and a 9178x2470 source:

```
GET /assets/<id>?width=400                      → 200
GET /assets/<id>?width=400&format=webp          → 400 ILLEGAL_ASSET_TRANSFORMATION
GET /assets/<id>?width=400&quality=80           → 400 ILLEGAL_ASSET_TRANSFORMATION
```

This is working as designed. `assertTransformsAllowed()` projects size through every
pipeline step and `resolvePreset()` places `toFormat` before `resize`, so once
`format` or `quality` is present the untouched source dimensions are what get
measured against the output cap. The docs state this explicitly ("Operations that
leave the dimensions unchanged, such as `blur`, are checked too"). #28103 raised it,
#28111 addressed it by raising the default so the output cap matches the source cap.

The remaining gap is that nothing stops such a source entering the library in the
first place. Aligning the two caps is a mitigation, not prevention: any image above
whichever cap you choose still lands, and silently loses webp/quality delivery. In
our case 4,288 of 193,644 images (~2.2%) sit above 6000px on an axis, the largest
being 15273x11696.

## Why a hook is not a good substitute

`FilesService.uploadOne()` creates the row, streams bytes to disk, and only then runs
`extractMetadata()` to learn width/height. The one event emitted is
`emitter.emitAction('files.upload')` — an action, after the write, not awaited.
`filter('files.create')` runs before the bytes exist and so has no dimensions to
test.

There is therefore no extension point where dimensions are known and the request can
still be refused. The best an extension can do is delete or rewrite the file *after*
a successful 200, which is visibly wrong to the editor. Enforcement has to live where
`FILES_MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE` already lives.

## Precedent

Both existing upload guards arrived as feature requests and were accepted:

- #18735 — Add env var for max file upload size (`FILES_MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE`)
- #18736 — Add support for `FILES_MIME_TYPE_ALLOW_LIST`

This is the same shape of control, on the axis the asset pipeline already cares about.

## Additional context

Directus 12.2.0, self-hosted, S3 storage adapter.

### Describe the Bug


`getService()` exists so that writes to a system collection reach the service that enforces that collection's
invariants. Its own documentation says so, at
[api/src/utils/get-service.ts:30-33](api/src/utils/get-service.ts#L30-L33):

```
Select the correct service for the given collection. This allows the individual services to run
their custom checks (f.e. it allows `UsersService` to prevent updating TFA secret from outside).
```

Six call sites build an `ItemsService` directly for a collection that may be a system collection, so those checks never
run.

Collection taken from a stored row:

- [api/src/services/revisions.ts:20](api/src/services/revisions.ts#L20) in `revert()`
- [api/src/services/versions.ts:488](api/src/services/versions.ts#L488) in `promote()`

Collection taken from caller-supplied operation options:

- [api/src/operations/item-create/index.ts:31](api/src/operations/item-create/index.ts#L31)
- [api/src/operations/item-read/index.ts:33](api/src/operations/item-read/index.ts#L33)
- [api/src/operations/item-update/index.ts:37](api/src/operations/item-update/index.ts#L37)
- [api/src/operations/item-delete/index.ts:33](api/src/operations/item-delete/index.ts#L33)

Every other site that builds an `ItemsService` from a caller-supplied collection name rejects system collections first,
which is what makes the four flow operations the outlier: [controllers/items.ts:22](api/src/controllers/items.ts#L22)
plus six sibling handlers, [websocket/handlers/items.ts:35](api/src/websocket/handlers/items.ts#L35), and
[ai/tools/items/index.ts:82](api/src/ai/tools/items/index.ts#L82).

### What gets skipped

More than the `UsersService` field guards:

- `UsersService`: password policy validation, email validation and uniqueness, and the `UserIntegrityCheckFlag` handling
  that enforces seat limits and the remaining-administrator count
- `PoliciesService` and `PermissionsService`: `clearCaches()`, leaving the permission cache stale after a write, and the
  `custom_permission_rules_enabled` entitlement check
- `PermissionsService.readByQuery`: entitlement filtering and app-minimal-permission merging on reads
- `getService()` itself: the `ForbiddenError` it raises for `directus_*` collections absent from its switch

### Two observable consequences

**Reverting a `directus_users` revision destroys the password.** Revision snapshots are captured through the
collection's read pipeline at [items.ts:908-910](api/src/services/items.ts#L908-L910), so `conceal` stores `password` as
the literal `**********` ([payload.ts:119-122](api/src/services/payload.ts#L119-L122)). `revert()` writes that snapshot
back through raw `ItemsService`, where the `hash` special hashes the placeholder. The account's password becomes the
string `**********`. This needs no attacker: it happens on a legitimate administrator revert.

**Promote can write `tfa_secret`.** `PATCH /users/{id}` refuses `tfa_secret` for every caller including administrators
([users.ts:308-310](api/src/services/users.ts#L308-L310)), and clearing another user's TFA via
`POST /users/{pk}/tfa/disable` requires admin ([controllers/users.ts:442](api/src/controllers/users.ts#L442)). Promote
reaches the field regardless. Because `tfa_secret` carries `conceal` only, the supplied value is stored verbatim and
accepted by `TFAService.verifyOTP`.

Related, and not fixed by the routing change: the version save path prepares its delta against `directus_versions`
rather than the target collection ([versions.ts:320-330](api/src/services/versions.ts#L320-L330)), so `hash` and
`conceal` fields are stored unprocessed in `directus_versions.delta`. For `directus_users` that is `password` and
`tfa_secret` in cleartext, readable by anyone with read access to versions. See the open design question below.

### To Reproduce

All steps are performed as an administrator. Create a second user, `victim@example.com`, with a known password.

**Revert destroying a password:**

1. As admin, `PATCH /users/{victim_id}` with `{"first_name":"Changed"}` to generate a revision.
2. `GET /revisions?filter[collection][_eq]=directus_users&filter[item][_eq]={victim_id}` and note the revision id. Its
   `data.password` is the literal `**********`.
3. `POST /utils/revert/{revision_id}`. Returns 204.
4. `POST /auth/login` as the victim with their original password. Returns 401.
5. `POST /auth/login` as the victim with the password `**********`. Returns 200.

Expected: reverting a non-credential field change does not alter the password. Actual: the password is replaced with a
publicly known string.

**Version delta storing credentials in cleartext, and promote writing `tfa_secret`:**

1. As admin, enable Content Versioning on `directus_users` (`PATCH /collections/directus_users` with
   `{"meta":{"versioning":true}}`).
2. `POST /versions` with `{"collection":"directus_users","item":"{victim_id}","key":"repro"}`.
3. `POST /versions/{version_id}/save` with `{"password":"ChosenPassword123!","tfa_secret":"JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP"}`.
4. Read the row: `directus_versions.delta` holds both values verbatim, unhashed and unconcealed.
5. `GET /versions/{version_id}/compare`, take `mainHash`, then `POST /versions/{version_id}/promote` with it.
6. The victim's `tfa_secret` is now the supplied value, and login requires an OTP generated from it. The equivalent
   `PATCH /users/{victim_id}` with `{"tfa_secret":"..."}` returns 400 for the same administrator.

Expected: `tfa_secret` is refused on this path as it is on the direct one, and credential fields are not stored in
cleartext in `directus_versions`. Actual: both occur.

### Directus Version

v12.3.0

### Hosting Strategy

Self-Hosted (Docker Image)

### Database

any

## Describe the Bug

When I AI-translate multiple fields into a language that does not yet have a translation row, Directus can create multiple local rows for that target language.

The translated title and content appear correctly in the editor, but saving fails validation against one of the hidden incomplete rows. In my case the error was:

> Translations → English → Title: Value is required

Each streamed field is applied synchronously. The relation row created for the first field is not visible through the updated v-model value until the next Vue update cycle, so subsequent fields can create additional rows.

## To Reproduce

1. Configure a standard translations interface with a required title field.
2. Open an item without a translation for the target language.
3. Select multiple fields for AI translation.
4. Translate into the missing language.
5. Save the item.

A single target-language row should be created and populated. Instead, multiple target-language rows can be created and validation fails on an incomplete duplicate.

I verified the diagnosis by applying a local image patch that waits for the relation update between streamed fields; translating and saving then worked successfully.

## Directus Version

12.2.0

Self-Hosted (Custom)

### Describe the Bug

When a non-admin edits a **content version**, the Studio makes every **readable** field editable, regardless of the user's **update** field permissions. Field-level access is deferred to promote time by design (see the risk note on #26815). The problem is what happens when that deferred check fails: the offending key is already persisted in `directus_versions.delta`, and there is no supported way to take it back out.

The result is a version that is permanently stuck. `POST /versions/:pk/promote` returns `FORBIDDEN` for the whole delta, and neither of the two write paths onto a version can remove the key. The user cannot publish their work, and cannot fix it themselves.

**Chain of behaviour (v12.2.0):**

1. **App — fields are gated on `read`, never on `update`, while editing a version.**
   `app/src/composables/use-permissions/item/lib/get-fields.ts` filters the field list by the `read` permission, then returns early for versions before any `readonly` / `non_editable` flag is applied:

   ```ts
   const readableFields = getPermission(collectionValue, 'read')?.fields;
   if (readableFields && !readableFields.includes('*')) {
     fields = fields.filter((field) => readableFields.includes(field.field));
   }

   // Version editing bypasses underlying collection write permissions entirely.
   // Field-level access is enforced by the backend at promote time.
   if (unref(isVersion)) return fields;
   ```

   `is-action-allowed.ts` does the same for the update action (`if (action === 'update' && unref(isVersion)) return true;`). So a field that is read-yes / update-no renders as a normal editable input inside a version, with no visual signal that it can never be published.

2. **API — the save endpoint accepts it, unchecked.**
   `VersionsService.save()` writes the merged delta through a sudo service, so nothing rejects the key at save time:

   ```ts
   const finalVersionDelta = assign({}, existingDelta, revisionDelta);

   const sudoService = new ItemsService(this.collection, {
     knex: this.knex,
     schema: this.schema,
     accountability: { ...this.accountability!, admin: true },
   });

   await sudoService.updateOne(key, { delta: finalVersionDelta });
   ```

   The user gets a successful save and believes the work is stored.

3. **API — promote validates the entire accumulated delta.**
   `VersionsService.promote()` passes the whole `rawDelta` to `itemsService.updateOne()` under the user's own accountability, so `processPayload` raises `createFieldsForbiddenError` for any key outside the update permission's `fields` list. One non-updatable key fails the publish of every other change in the version.

4. **No repair path exists.** This is the part that turns an error into a dead end:
   - `POST /versions/:pk/save` **merges only** (`assign({}, existingDelta, revisionDelta)`). Sending `null`, `undefined`, or omitting the key cannot delete it.
   - `PATCH /versions/:pk` cannot touch the delta at all. `VersionsService.updateMany()` validates the payload against a Joi schema of `key`, `name`, `item`, so any request containing `delta` fails with `InvalidPayloadError`.
   - That leaves only two admin-side escapes: a field-subset promote (`POST /versions/:pk/promote` with a `fields` allowlist), or deleting the version and losing the draft. Neither is available to the editor who owns the draft, and the first is not exposed anywhere in the Studio.

### To Reproduce

1. Enable Content Versioning on a collection, for example `articles` with fields `title` and `internal_note`.
2. Create a policy with:
   - `read` on `articles`, fields: `title`, `internal_note`
   - `update` on `articles`, fields: `title` **only**
   - full create/read/update on `directus_versions`
3. Assign it to a non-admin user, and create an item as an admin.
4. As the non-admin, open the item, create a draft version, and edit **both** `title` and `internal_note`. Note that `internal_note` renders as a normal editable field, with no read-only indicator.
5. Save the version. It succeeds (HTTP 200), and `directus_versions.delta` now holds both keys.
6. Publish the version → `FORBIDDEN`. The legitimate `title` change cannot be published either.
7. Try to recover as that user:
   - re-save the version with only `{"title": "..."}` → still 200, but the delta keeps `internal_note`, and publish still fails
   - `PATCH /versions/:pk` with `{"delta": {"title": "..."}}` → `InvalidPayloadError` ("delta is not allowed")

   The version is unrecoverable without an administrator.

### Expected Behaviour

Any one of these would close the trap; the first two seem the most useful:

1. **Gate editability on `update` inside versions too.** Apply the same `readonly` / `non_editable` treatment in `getFields()` when `isVersion` is true, so a non-updatable field is visibly locked and never reaches a delta. This is a partial revert of the deferral introduced in #26815, which was aimed at *conditional* (item-level) update rules, not field-level ones. Item-level conditions can still be deferred to promote; field-level lists do not depend on the item's state and can be resolved up front.
2. **Reject non-updatable fields at save time**, so the delta cannot accumulate a key that can never be promoted. Failing fast at save is far better than failing at publish.
3. **Give the delta a repair path** — allow removing keys from a version delta, either by honouring an explicit delete/unset in `POST /versions/:pk/save` or by permitting `delta` in `PATCH /versions/:pk` for users with update permission on `directus_versions`.
4. At minimum, surface the field-subset promote in the Studio and name the blocking fields in the error, so an editor can publish the rest of their work.

### Impact

We hit this on a production instance with ~590 event editors sharing one policy. A field the editors can read but not update was captured in a draft delta, and the editor was locked out of publishing the whole draft until an administrator promoted a hand-picked field subset and deleted the version. Any editor whose draft touches a read-only field reproduces it, and there is nothing the editor can do about it.

Granting update on the specific field only closes that one instance. On the policy in question, 18 further fields remain readable-but-not-updatable, and deliberately so: `status`, `start_date`, `finish_date`, `name`, `slug`, `id`, `country_id`, `categories`. Those are exactly the fields an editor must be able to see and must not be able to change, so the trap cannot be designed away at the policy level. Any read/update asymmetry, which is the normal reason to use field-level permissions at all, is enough to reproduce it.

### Directus Version

v12.2.0

### Hosting Strategy

Self-Hosted (Docker Image)

### Database

Aurora Mysql 8

### Describe the Bug

Four independent findings from auditing the remaining `directus_*` collections not covered by #27945/#27956/#27970. Grouped into one issue since they came out of the same audit pass, not because they're related to each other, happy to split into separate PRs per group if that's easier to review (see the note at the bottom).

1. `directus_notifications.id` is typed `string`, the column is an auto-incrementing integer.

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/api/src/database/migrations/20211118A-add-notifications.ts#L6-L14

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/packages/types/src/notifications.ts#L3-L13

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/sdk/src/schema/notification.ts#L5-L17

`id` should be `number` in both files. `status` and `timestamp` are also wrong in `packages/types/src/notifications.ts`: `status` has no `.notNullable()`, and `timestamp` was explicitly flipped nullable by a later migration:

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/api/src/database/migrations/20220801A-update-notifications-timestamp-column.ts#L4-L10

`sdk/src/schema/notification.ts` already has `status`/`timestamp` right, only `id` needs fixing there.

2. `sdk/src/schema/permission.ts`'s `DirectusPermission.policy` is typed nullable, the column is `NOT NULL`.

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/api/src/database/migrations/20240806A-permissions-policies.ts#L154-L167

Every null `role` is backfilled to `PUBLIC_POLICY_ID` before `policy` is populated and `dropNullable('policy')` is called, so every real row is guaranteed a policy:

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/sdk/src/schema/permission.ts#L5-L17

`packages/types/src/permissions.ts`'s `Permission.policy` is also typed nullable, but that one should stay untouched. That type is shared with synthetic, non-DB-backed permission objects the access-control engine builds in memory (`packages/system-data/src/app-access-permissions/index.ts`, `api/src/permissions/utils/default-permission.ts`, `api/src/permissions/utils/get-permissions-for-share.ts`), and those legitimately have no policy. None of them are ever served through the `/permissions` endpoint.

3. `@directus/sdk` shapes for `directus_extensions` and `directus_fields` are missing fields present in the API output.

`DirectusExtension['schema']` is missing most of `ApiOutput.schema` shape:

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/sdk/src/schema/extension.ts#L3-L18

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/packages/types/src/extensions/app-extension-config.ts#L74-L79

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/packages/types/src/extensions/app-extension-config.ts#L94-L129

`ExtensionSchema` only carries `type`/`local`/`version` out of the full `Partial<Extension>` shape. `path`, `name`, `entrypoint`, `host`, and the bundle-only `partial`/`entries` are all absent, and `Partial<>` means every field (including `type`/`local`) is actually optional, which `ExtensionSchema` doesn't reflect either.

`DirectusField['meta']` is missing `system` and `clear_hidden_value_on_save`:

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/sdk/src/schema/field.ts#L7-L32

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/packages/system-data/src/types.ts#L69-L91

`system` marks system-defined fields and `clear_hidden_value_on_save` is a real per-field flag used by the app; both are absent from the sdk's `meta`.

Same file, `schema` sub-object marks driver-conditional columns as always present:

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/sdk/src/schema/field.ts#L33-L53

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/packages/schema/src/types/column.ts#L1-L26

`schema` (Postgres only) and `comment` (unsupported on SQLite/MSSQL) are optional in `Column` type for exactly that reason; the sdk types both as always-present. `generation_expression` is also narrowed to `unknown | null` in the sdk instead of `string | null`, and made required instead of optional.

4. `collection`-name FK fields typed as bare `string` even though `keyof CompleteSchema<Schema>` already exists.

`directus_collections`'s primary key is the collection name itself, so any field that references a collection by name should be typed against the known collection keys, not a bare `string`. `CompleteSchema<Schema>` already exists and resolves this correctly, it's just never applied to these fields:

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/sdk/src/types/schema.ts#L80-L89

`notification.ts` and `permission.ts` (both already touched by finding 1 and 2 above), and `field.ts` (already touched by finding 3 above) all have this same gap, self-flagged with a `// TODO keyof complete schema` comment.

3 further fields have the same gap and aren't touched by any other finding here, 2 of them self-flagged the same way:

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/sdk/src/schema/collection.ts#L1-L12

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/sdk/src/schema/revision.ts#L11

https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/d87981b99d2e7916905ac797fda79f33dc01190b/sdk/src/schema/activity.ts#L15 (not self-flagged, same gap)

`relation.ts`'s 4 occurrences, plus `version.ts`, `comment.ts`, and `preset.ts`, already had this same gap but are excluded here, all four are already fixed to `keyof CompleteSchema<Schema>` directly in open PRs #27970 and #27956.

## Describe the Bug

Fields marked with the `encrypt` special (for example `directus_deployments.credentials`) are redacted to the literal string `'**********'` on read, but the SDK's collection schema types them with a single shape used for both reading and writing. This forces a choice between two inaccurate options:

- Type the field as `Record<string, any>` (its write shape). This is inaccurate for `readItem`/`readItems`, which will actually return `'**********' | null`.
- Type the field as `'**********' | null` (its read shape). This is inaccurate for `createItem`/`updateItem`, which require the real, provider-specific object.

`directus_deployments.credentials` is the clearest case because the read and write shapes are structurally different types, `'**********' | null` versus `Record<string, any>`, so no single field type can satisfy both `readItem` and `createItem`/`updateItem` callers without an assertion or cast. The same mismatch affects other `encrypt`-special fields in `directus_settings` (`ai_<provider>_api_key`, `license_key`, `license_token`), though those are lower impact since read and write are both `string | null` there.

An initial attempt at #27945 typed `DirectusDeployment.credentials` as `'**********' | null` (matching read behavior) and gave `createDeployment`/`updateDeployment` their own parameter types that `Omit` the field and replace it with the real input shape. That approach was reverted during review in favor of keeping `credentials` typed as `Record<string, any>` (its write shape), since it only patched one command pair and there is no general mechanism in the SDK for a "specials" field to declare a different read type versus write type on the generic `readItem`/`createItem`/`updateItem`/`updateItems` commands. The solution for this issue should address whether a generic fix for this be implemented rather than attempted per-field.

## To Reproduce

1. In `sdk/src/schema/deployment.ts`, note that `DirectusDeployment.credentials` is typed `Record<string, any>`.
2. Call `readItem('directus_deployments', id, { fields: ['credentials'] })`. The inferred `credentials` type is `Record<string, any>`, but the API actually returns the literal string `'**********'` for any authenticated request.

Part of the spec drift audit tracked in directus/directus#27700.

## Scope

`packages/specs/src/paths/assets/` only documents `GET /assets/{id}`. Two POST routes on the same controller that return a zip archive have no spec coverage at all: bundling them into one PR is reasonable since they share the same response shape and controller.

## Routes to document

`api/src/controllers/assets.ts`

* `POST /assets/folder/:pk`: archives every file within folder `pk` (recursively) into a zip and streams it back. No request body. Response is `application/zip` with a `Content-Disposition: attachment` header naming the file `folder-<folder name>-<timestamp>.zip`.
* `POST /assets/files/`: archives an arbitrary set of files into a zip and streams it back. Request body is `{ "ids": string[] }` (UUIDs, min length 1; validated with `zod`, rejects with `InvalidPayloadError` on a bad shape). Response is `application/zip` with a `Content-Disposition: attachment` header naming the file `files-<timestamp>.zip`.

Both routes run through `checkIsLocked('assets')` and `useCollection('directus_files')`, and both construct an `AssetsService` with the caller's own `accountability` - access to the underlying files is governed by normal RBAC read permissions on `directus_files` (and, for the folder route, `directus_folders`), not a hardcoded check. This is a documentation gap only, not a security/RBAC bug.

## Implementation notes

Add a new path file, e.g. `packages/specs/src/paths/assets/folder.yaml` and  `packages/specs/src/paths/assets/files.yaml`, registered in `openapi.yaml` as `/assets/folder/{pk}` and `/assets/files`. Both should use the `Assets` tag.

* `POST /assets/files/`: set `x-collection: directus_files`, following the operation-level override pattern established for `GET /assets/{id}` in directus/directus#27883.
* `POST /assets/folder/{pk}`: set `x-collection: directus_folders`. `FoldersService.buildTree()` calls `validateAccess` on the root folder id and throws `ForbiddenError` if `directus_folders:read` is missing - that's the only hard gate on the route. The files themselves are filtered silently by `directus_files` read permissions (missing access just omits files from the zip rather than blocking the request), so `directus_folders` is the correct single collection to gate on.

Response schema: `application/zip`, `type: string`, `format: binary` (there's no existing zip response schema to reuse; the closest precedent is the `text/plain` `type: string` response already used for `GET /assets/{id}`).

For `POST /assets/files/`: document the `ids` request body per the zod schema in the controller (`array of string, uuid, min 1`), and the `InvalidPayloadError` (400) response for a malformed body.

## Verification

Run `pnpm validate` in `packages/specs` and confirm it passes clean. Verify in a Swagger viewer that both new path entries appear under the `Assets` tag with correct request/response documentation.

# O2M Nested Fields Not Returned When Role Has Multiple Policies (Directus 11.17.3)

## Summary

When a role has multiple policies attached (custom policy + public policy inheritance), **One-to-Many (o2m) nested relationship fields are silently excluded from API responses**, even when both policies grant explicit read permissions to the related collection.

This works correctly when:
- Using ONLY the public policy (unauthenticated requests)
- Using a role with ONLY ONE policy

This fails when:
- A role has 2+ policies attached via `directus_access`
- Querying nested o2m fields in the `fields` parameter

## Environment

- **Directus Version**: 11.17.3
- **Database**: PostgreSQL
- **Node Version**: (via Docker)
- **Installation**: Docker deployment

## Reproduction Steps

### 1. Database Schema

**Parent Collection**: `software`  
**Child Collection**: `software_pricing_plans`  
**Relationship**: O2M via `software_pricing_plans.software` → `software.id`

```sql
-- Relationship
SELECT many_collection, many_field, one_collection, one_field 
FROM directus_relations 
WHERE many_collection = 'software_pricing_plans';

-- Result:
-- many_collection: software_pricing_plans
-- many_field: software
-- one_collection: software
-- one_field: pricing_plans
```

### 2. Permission Setup

**Public Policy** (UUID: `abf8a154-5b1c-4a46-ac9c-7300570f4f17`):
```sql
-- software collection
INSERT INTO directus_permissions (collection, action, fields, policy) 
VALUES ('software', 'read', '*', 'abf8a154-5b1c-4a46-ac9c-7300570f4f17');

-- software_pricing_plans collection  
INSERT INTO directus_permissions (collection, action, fields, policy)
VALUES ('software_pricing_plans', 'read', '*', 'abf8a154-5b1c-4a46-ac9c-7300570f4f17');
```

**Basic Policy** (UUID: `c284f76c-f8cf-4866-9d48-1bab19e174c2`):
```sql
-- software collection
INSERT INTO directus_permissions (collection, action, fields, policy)
VALUES ('software', 'read', '*', 'c284f76c-f8cf-4866-9d48-1bab19e174c2');

-- software_pricing_plans collection
INSERT INTO directus_permissions (collection, action, fields, policy)
VALUES ('software_pricing_plans', 'read', '*', 'c284f76c-f8cf-4866-9d48-1bab19e174c2');
```

**Basic Role** (UUID: `dccb7894-1e52-4c1e-b2a2-6465dda5956f`) has BOTH policies:
```sql
INSERT INTO directus_access (role, policy, sort) VALUES
  ('dccb7894-1e52-4c1e-b2a2-6465dda5956f', 'c284f76c-f8cf-4866-9d48-1bab19e174c2', 1),
  ('dccb7894-1e52-4c1e-b2a2-6465dda5956f', 'abf8a154-5b1c-4a46-ac9c-7300570f4f17', 2);
```

### 3. API Request

```bash
# Request nested pricing_plans
GET /items/software?filter[product_slug][_eq]=Impact.com&fields=id,product_name,pricing_plans.id,pricing_plans.plan_name,pricing_plans.status&limit=1
```

### 4. Expected vs Actual Behavior

**Expected** (when unauthenticated / public-only):
```json
{
  "data": [{
    "id": "c96c73d6-6fea-46ce-9a72-260e2aa02cb1",
    "product_name": "Impact.com",
    "pricing_plans": [
      {
        "id": 123,
        "plan_name": "Starter",
        "status": "published"
      }
    ]
  }]
}
```

**Actual** (when authenticated as Basic user):
```json
{
  "data": [{
    "id": "c96c73d6-6fea-46ce-9a72-260e2aa02cb1",
    "product_name": "Impact.com"
    // pricing_plans field completely missing!
  }]
}
```

## Debugging Steps Performed

### ✅ Confirmed Working Scenarios

1. **Unauthenticated (public policy only)**: Returns `pricing_plans` correctly
2. **Admin token**: Returns `pricing_plans` correctly
3. **Other o2m fields** (features, integrations, social_links): Work correctly for Basic role

### ❌ Confirmed Failing Scenarios

1. **Basic role with both policies**: `pricing_plans` silently excluded
2. **Even after Directus restart**: Issue persists
3. **Even after logout + fresh JWT**: Issue persists

### 🔍 Verified Configuration

```sql
-- Confirmed permissions exist for both policies
SELECT p.id, p.collection, p.action, p.fields, pol.name 
FROM directus_permissions p
JOIN directus_policies pol ON p.policy = pol.id
WHERE p.collection IN ('software', 'software_pricing_plans')
ORDER BY pol.name, p.collection;

-- Result: Both policies have read permissions with fields='*'

-- Confirmed role has both policies attached
SELECT r.name, p.name as policy_name, da.sort
FROM directus_roles r
JOIN directus_access da ON r.id = da.role
JOIN directus_policies p ON da.policy = p.id
WHERE r.name = 'Basic'
ORDER BY da.sort;

-- Result: Basic (sort=1), $t:public_label (sort=2)

-- Confirmed relationship exists
SELECT * FROM directus_relations 
WHERE many_collection = 'software_pricing_plans';

-- Result: Relationship correctly configured
```

### 🧪 Experiments Performed

1. **Removed public policy inheritance** → Still failed
2. **Removed Basic policy, kept only public** → Could not test (schema-sync blocked restart)
3. **Deleted all non-public permissions** → Still failed
4. **Multiple Directus restarts** → No change
5. **Hard browser cache clear + incognito** → No change

## Additional Context

- **Other nested o2m fields work**: `features`, `integrations`, `social_links` are all returned correctly
- **Only `pricing_plans` is affected**: Same permission structure, different behavior
- **No validation rules or filters**: Permissions have clean `permissions: {}` and `validation: null`
- **No blocking flows**: Confirmed no hooks interfering with this collection
- **Directus logs show no errors**: Request completes successfully with 200 status

## Hypothesis

Policy inheritance in Directus 11.x may not properly apply to nested o2m fields when a role has multiple policies. The permission check might be:
1. Only evaluating the first policy (sort=1)
2. OR requiring explicit permissions in BOTH policies
3. OR failing to merge permission sets for nested relationships

## Workaround

As a temporary solution, we're considering fetching data via an admin token and manually filtering in the application layer, but this bypasses Directus' permission system entirely.

## Request

Is this a known limitation of multi-policy roles in Directus 11.x? If so, what is the recommended approach for:
1. Roles that need custom permissions + public policy inheritance
2. Nested o2m field access with policy inheritance

Thank you for your help!

---

**Related Collections Schema**:
- `software`: Main entity collection
- `software_pricing_plans`: Pricing data (O2M relationship via `software` field)
- Both collections have identical permission structures across policies
- Only `pricing_plans` o2m field is affected; other o2m relationships work correctly

# Schema cache lock (`schemaCache--preparing`) has no TTL — a process killed mid-schema-build stalls the whole instance until `CACHE_SCHEMA_MAX_ITERATIONS`

### Describe the Bug

When Redis-backed caching is enabled, `getSchema()` coordinates schema
computation across processes using a Redis counter key
`<REDIS_LOCK_NAMESPACE>:schemaCache--preparing` (default namespace
`directus:lock`). This key is created with **no TTL/expiry** and is only ever
removed by (a) the owning process's `finally` block, or (b) the
`processId >= CACHE_SCHEMA_MAX_ITERATIONS` force-clear.

If the owning process (the one that gets `processId === 1`) is **force-killed**
after it increments the lock but before its `finally` runs `lock.delete()` — e.g.
OOM kill, `SIGKILL`, container/host termination, or the worker dying while a
long-running operation holds the event loop — the counter is orphaned. Because it
has no TTL, it never expires. Every subsequent process then:

1. increments the counter → gets `processId >= 2`, so it is never the owner;
2. waits on the `schemaCache--done` message-bus event that the dead owner will
   never publish;
3. times out after `CACHE_SCHEMA_SYNC_TIMEOUT`, retries up to `MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3`;
4. throws `Failed to get Schema information: hit infinite loop`.

The instance only recovers once the counter — incremented request by request —
reaches `CACHE_SCHEMA_MAX_ITERATIONS` (default **100**) and the key is deleted.
With the default that is ~100 accumulated failed requests of continuous downtime.

Note that only processes with an **empty in-memory schema cache** are affected:
`getSchema()` returns early from `getMemorySchemaCache()` before it touches the
lock, so a long-lived warm process keeps working. But any process that
(re)starts, is scaled in, is redeployed, or has just had its cache purged
(`CACHE_AUTO_PURGE`) during the stuck-lock window hits the loop. In a
horizontally-scaled deployment this is severe: the lock lives in the **shared**
Redis, so every newly-started replica boots with an empty in-memory cache and
immediately re-hits the same poisoned key — the deployment cannot heal itself by
restarting nodes.

### Impact — this affects the whole API, not just the Studio

`getSchema()` runs inside the **global** `schema` middleware
(`app.use(schema)` in `api/src/app.ts`), which is mounted before every data
router (`/items`, `/graphql`, `/files`, …) and before `/server`. So while the
lock is stuck:

- every REST and GraphQL request fails with a 500 (the Studio is a client of this
  same API, so it is unusable too — its static assets load, but every call fails);
- `GET /server/health` is behind the same middleware and therefore also fails, so
  any load balancer / orchestrator health check pointed at `/server/health` will
  consider the node unhealthy and may recycle it — which, per the shared-cache
  point above, makes the outage worse rather than better.
- `GET /server/ping` is registered *before* the schema middleware and keeps
  responding, which is the only easy way to tell the process is alive at all.

### To Reproduce

With Redis caching enabled (`CACHE_ENABLED=true`, `CACHE_STORE=redis`,
`REDIS=redis://…`) and schema caching on (the default):

1. Start Directus and serve at least one request so a schema is computed.
2. Simulate the orphaned owner by injecting the counter directly into Redis
   (equivalent to the owner dying before its `finally` runs). A value `>= 1`
   ensures the next increment never returns `1`, so no process becomes owner:
   ```
   redis-cli SET directus:lock:schemaCache--preparing 1
   ```
3. Restart the Directus process. This empties its in-memory schema cache while the
   injected key survives in Redis.
4. Observe:
   - `GET /server/health` → 503
   - `GET /items/<any collection>` → 500, log line
     `Failed to get Schema information: hit infinite loop`
   - `GET /server/ping` → still `pong`
5. `redis-cli DEL directus:lock:schemaCache--preparing` → the next request
   recovers immediately, confirming the orphaned, no-TTL key is the sole cause.

A "natural" variant without injection: force a schema computation and `SIGKILL`
the process mid-build (so no graceful shutdown runs the cleanup), then restart —
the same leftover counter remains.

### Root cause (source references)

- `api/src/utils/get-schema.ts` — the counter is created via `lock.increment()`;
  the only cleanup is `lock.delete()` in the `finally`, which is skipped when the
  process is force-killed:
  ```ts
  const lockKey = 'schemaCache--preparing';
  const processId = await lock.increment(lockKey);
  if (processId >= (env['CACHE_SCHEMA_MAX_ITERATIONS'] as number)) {
      await lock.delete(lockKey);
  }
  const currentProcessShouldHandleOperation = processId === 1;
  // non-owners: race(timeout(CACHE_SCHEMA_SYNC_TIMEOUT), bus.subscribe(...))
  //             .catch(() => getSchema(options, attempt + 1)) // MAX_ATTEMPTS=3 -> throws
  ...
  } finally {
      await bus.publish(messageKey, { schema });
      await lock.delete(lockKey); // skipped on force-kill
  }
  ```
- `api/src/lock/lib/use-lock.ts` — `useLock()` builds the KV with
  `createKv({ type: 'redis', …, namespace: 'directus:lock' })` and passes **no
  `ttl`**.
- `packages/memory/src/kv/lib/redis.ts` — `increment()` is
  `return await this.redis.incrby(withNamespace(key, this.namespace), amount)`:
  a plain `INCRBY` with no `EXPIRE`. This class only applies a TTL inside `set()`
  (via `'PX', this.ttl`), and only when a `ttl` is configured — which the lock
  instance never is. So the counter key is created with no expiry.

### Possible fix (any one of)

1. **Give the lock a TTL** so an orphaned owner self-clears in seconds instead of
   depending on `CACHE_SCHEMA_MAX_ITERATIONS`. Have `useLock()` pass a `ttl` to
   `createKv`, and make `KvRedis.increment()` set an expiry when it creates the
   key (e.g. `INCR` followed by `PEXPIRE key <ttl> NX`, or a small Lua script that
   sets the TTL on first increment). A TTL of a few multiples of
   `CACHE_SCHEMA_SYNC_TIMEOUT` would be a safe upper bound on any schema build.
2. **Use the TTL-based lock helpers that already exist.** `packages/memory/src/kv/lib/redis.ts`
   already provides `acquireLock` / `usingLock` (Redlock-based, auto-expiring,
   auto-releasing) which are not currently used by `get-schema.ts`. Coordinating
   the schema build through a real auto-expiring lock eliminates the orphaned-lock
   failure class entirely.
3. At minimum, **lower the default `CACHE_SCHEMA_MAX_ITERATIONS`** and document
   that it is currently the *only* recovery path for a crashed schema owner — 100
   accumulated failed requests is a very long outage for a hard-to-avoid crash.

### Environment

- Directus: reproduced on 11.17.1; the lock code is unchanged through 12.1.1 and
  `main` at the time of writing.
- Cache/lock store: any Redis-compatible server.
- Deployment: most impactful on a multi-process / multi-replica deployment sharing
  one Redis, but the mechanism reproduces on a single node.

There is no ~~distinction between what an authenticated caller with broad permissions receives and what a public/unauthenticated caller actually receives~~ way specify a role without being a user with that role.
outdated: Because the public role's permissions are typically narrower (e.g. it may be able to read `directus_files` but not `directus_folders` or `directus_users`), a public request's real response replaces related-record objects with a bare scalar (the related record's primary key) instead of the nested object the spec's `Schema` documents. A caller relying on the spec's "Example Value" in Swagger/Swagger Editor will see fields and relations that are never actually returned to them. ### Concrete example ```yaml # Authenticated request with access to the full Schema for Folders and Users Files: type: object properties: … folder: oneOf: - type: string - $ref: '#/components/schemas/Folders' nullable: true uploaded_by: oneOf: - type: string - $ref: '#/components/schemas/Users' # Public request: the public policy has no access to Folders or Users, # so only the bare uuid is returned for each relation Files_Public: type: object properties: … folder: nullable: true type: string format: uuid uploaded_by: nullable: true type: string format: uuid … additionalProperties: false ``` Today the spec has only the first (`Files`) shape; there is no `Files_Public` equivalent, so a public caller has no accurate documentation of what they'll actually receive. ### Affected paths Any operation whose response references a collection `Schema` and that is reachable by the public role: primarily `GET`/`SEARCH` on `/items/{collection}` and the equivalent system-collection read paths, wherever the public role has been granted access. Part of the spec drift audit tracked in directus/directus#27700. ## Problem The 21 component files in `packages/specs/src/components/` document the read shapes returned by `@directus/api`. They are referenced by every `requestBody` and response schema in `packages/specs/src/paths/`, so an error in a component propagates everywhere it is used. Follow-up from review discussion on directus/directus#27883. While addressing that PR, a related gap was flagged in [this comment](<https://github.com/directus/directus/pull/27883#discussion_r3583685830>):

This issue documents that gap.

Part of the spec drift audit tracked in directus/directus#27700

## Problem

The dynamic (per-user) OAS spec generated by `GET /server/specs/oas` (`OASSpecsService.generatePaths()` in `api/src/services/specifications.ts`) decides whether to include an operation in a caller's spec purely by checking RBAC permissions against the operation's collection and action. A tag-level `x-authentication` escape hatch already exists (`packages/specs/src/openapi.yaml`, e.g. the `Schema` tag is `admin`-gated, `Utilities` is `user`-gated), but it's all-or-nothing per tag - every operation under the tag inherits the same requirement.

Several tags mix operations that have different real auth requirements:

* **Collections, Fields, Relations, Extensions**: mutating operations (create/update/delete a collection, field, relation, or extension) are enforced as admin-only directly in the service layer (e.g. `api/src/services/collections.ts` throws `ForbiddenError` unless `accountability.admin === true`, independent of whatever RBAC permissions exist on `directus_collections`/`directus_fields`/`directus_relations`). GET operations on the same tags are not admin-gated.
* **Comments**: all mutating operations require an authenticated (non-public) user (`api/src/services/comments.ts` - `if (!this.accountability?.user) throw new ForbiddenError()`), but GET is RBAC/public-permission driven like a normal collection.

Because the spec generator only asks "does this role/policy have an RBAC permission on this collection+action," a role that happens to hold full CRUD permissions on `directus_collections` (or `directus_fields`/`directus_relations`/`directus_extensions`) - which is a reasonable thing to grant for read/introspection purposes - will see `Update a Collection`/`Delete a Field`/etc. listed in its generated spec as available, and those operations could even be marked publicly accessible if a public permission happens to match by collection+action. In reality the API rejects the same non-admin request with a 403. The same problem applies to `Comments`: a public/no-user request could be shown as able to create, update, or delete a comment.

### Concrete example

A role granted full CRUD permission on `directus_fields` (reasonable to grant for schema introspection) will see `PATCH /fields/{collection}/{field}` and `DELETE /fields/{collection}/{field}` in its generated OAS spec, even though only true admins can actually call those endpoints.

### Affected paths

* Admin-only, RBAC-independent: `collections.yaml`, `collection.yaml`, `collection-fields.yaml`, `collection-field.yaml`, `relations.yaml`, `relation.yaml`, `extensions/update.yaml`, `extensions/update-bundle.yaml`
* Authenticated-user-only, RBAC-independent: `comments.yaml`, `comment.yaml`

## Implementation notes

Add a per-operation `x-authentication: admin | user` OAS extension (finer-grained than the existing per-tag one) to the operations listed above, and update `OASSpecsService.generatePaths()` (`api/src/services/specifications.ts`) so that:

1. An operation flagged `x-authentication: admin` is only included for `accountability.admin === true`, bypassing the RBAC permission check entirely.
2. An operation carrying any `x-authentication` level is never marked publicly accessible, even if a public permission coincidentally matches its collection+action.

## Verification

Run `pnpm --filter @directus/specs build` and `pnpm --filter @directus/api dev`. Hit `GET /server/specs/oas` as a non-admin role granted RBAC permissions on `directus_collections`/`directus_fields`/`directus_relations`/`directus_extensions` and confirm the admin-only mutating operations no longer appear in the generated spec. Confirm `Comments` mutations don't appear for a public/unauthenticated request.

## Discussion/Questions

The proposed fix can be scoped to the specs/api package to address the issue as discovered or it can be scoped to include preventing (or at least notifying) the user from applying roles/permissions to the Public user that violate the hard-coded requirements. I'll need to investigate how this message (found at `/admin/settings/roles/public`):

> The public role controls what API data is available to unauthenticated users or users without a role. Requests with the public role can not have app or admin access. If app or admin access are given to a policy assigned to the public role they will be ignored.

handles the ignored policies to understand the lift/scope if that's the decision made. I'm unsure if enhancing the message to explain each exception is warranted, especially since it will ultimately be hard to maintain an accurate message.

### Describe the Bug

I would like to raise this issue based on the behavior discussed in:

- https://github.com/directus/directus/issues/26689
- https://github.com/directus/directus/issues/27060
- https://github.com/directus/directus/issues/26838
- https://github.com/directus/directus/issues/26911
- https://github.com/directus/directus/issues/27404

As previously mentioned in the discussions:

> “To stay consistent we’ve decided to move forward with leaving disabled fields disabled — no interaction. However, to achieve what you need, you could take advantage of field permissions. This way the field turns to "non-editable" and you’re able to "Navigate to the item".”

Unfortunately, this approach does not work for our use case.

In our `orders` collection, we have a `client` relation. The client should remain editable under normal conditions, but once an invoice is associated with the order, the field must become read-only. At that point, users should still be able to open the client profile and inspect it, even if they can no longer change the relation.

The current behavior breaks this workflow. When the field becomes disabled, navigation to the related item is no longer possible. This is not acceptable for our case, because the user is not being granted edit access to the relation — they only need to view the linked record.

We also cannot solve this with permissions alone, because this is not a role-based access problem. It is a conditional UI behavior based on the state of the item itself. As Gerard noted [#27060](https://github.com/directus/directus/issues/27060#issuecomment-4204596978)_:

> We have 32 different roles and even more policies. This disabled setting was supposed to be for everyone regardless of their role or even being admin. So permissions isn't going to cut it. 

That is exactly the problem we are facing.

This request has been raised by many users, and the current responses do not address the real need in a way that works for us. I respectfully ask that this behavior be reconsidered, as it is a blocker for our client and prevents upgrading to newer Directus versions.

## Expected behavior

When a relation field becomes read-only due to a condition on the current item, users should still be able to navigate to the related item.

## Actual behavior

When the field is disabled, navigation to the related item is blocked, which breaks an existing workflow.

## Impact

This is a blocker for our client, and it directly affects our ability to upgrade to newer Directus versions.

Please reconsider supporting a state where relation fields can be **non-editable but still navigable**, especially when the disabled state is triggered by item conditions rather than permissions.


### Directus Version

v12.0.2

This endpoint manages content share records (`directus_shares`) and includes three special-purpose endpoints beyond standard CRUD: a public auth endpoint, an email invitation endpoint, and a public info endpoint. The non-standard endpoints and mixed authentication requirements make this one of the more complex undocumented paths.

## Routes to document

## Scope

The API implements the `SEARCH` HTTP method as an alternative to `GET` for complex filtered queries (passes a request body with `query` fields). It is currently undocumented on every endpoint. This is the broadest single gap in the spec: at least 16 paths are affected and every API consumer who relies on generated clients is missing this capability entirely.

## Routes to document

Add `SEARCH` operation objects to all of the following paths:

* `/collections`
* `/comments`
* `/dashboards`
* `/files`
* `/folders`
* `/items/{collection}`
* `/notifications`

* `/permissions`
* `/presets`
* `/revisions`
* `/roles`
* `/shares`
* `/translations`
* `/users`
* `/versions`

Each `SEARCH` operation accepts a request body with a `query` property (same shape accepted by GET query parameters) and returns the same response schema as the corresponding `GET` list operation.

## Implementation notes

Locate the existing path YAML files under `packages/specs/src/paths/` for each affected endpoint. Add a `search:` operation block alongside `get:` and `post:` following the pattern for list endpoints. The request body schema should reference or inline the `Query` component. Note: `/dashboards`, `/panels`, `/notifications`, `/translations`, and `/shares` may not yet have path files as those are being added in sibling issues. Coordinate or stack this PR on top of those if needed, or add the SEARCH block as part of each of those sibling PRs.

### Describe the Bug In v12, LicenseManager.initialize() runs during createApp() on every boot and wraps the entire licence initialisation in a Redis distributed lock (Redlock, via @directus/memory's usingLock). The critical section includes the outbound HTTP call to the license server (activate / refresh / update), which on first activation can take \~90 seconds. Because the lock is held for that long, when more than one Directus process boots at the same time against the same Redis, only the first acquires the lock. The others exhaust Redlock's (short, default) retry window and throw: ``` ExecutionError: The operation was unable to achieve a quorum during its retry window. at Redlock._execute (@sesamecare-oss/redlock/build/index.js:231:15) at async Redlock.acquire (@sesamecare-oss/redlock/build/index.js:152:41) at async Redlock.using (@sesamecare-oss/redlock/build/index.js:368:19) at async CacheRedis.usingLock (@directus/memory/dist/index.js:437:10) at async LicenseManager.initialize (@directus/api/dist/license/manager.js:60:4) at async createApp (@directus/api/dist/app.js:111:2) at async createServer (@directus/api/dist/server.js:27:35) at async Command.startServer (@directus/api/dist/server.js:119:17) This is an unhandled rejection in the boot path, so the process exits. The relevant source is [api/src/license/manager.ts](https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/v12.0.2/api/src/license/manager.ts) — initialize() runs its whole body inside this.store(cb) (i.e. useStore(LICENSE_NAMESPACE) → usingLock in [api/src/utils/store.ts](https://github.com/directus/directus/blob/v12.0.2/api/src/utils/store.ts)) and only releases after the licence HTTP call returns. ``` "Concurrent boot" happens in two common, legitimate configurations: PM2 cluster mode with PM2_INSTANCES > 1 (the official Docker image's ecosystem.config.cjs defaults to exec_mode: 'cluster'): each worker runs LicenseManager.initialize and they contend; the losing workers crash.
Multiple replicas/containers starting together (e.g. an ECS/Kubernetes rolling deployment that launches N tasks at once): all but one task crash and the deployment fails or rolls back.
Single-instance deployments are unaffected, which is why this is easy to miss in development. ### To Reproduce 1. Self-hosted Directus 12.0.2 with Redis configured (REDIS=...) and a LICENSE_KEY set (so boot performs activation). 2. Start two or more instances simultaneously against the same Redis. Either:
set PM2_INSTANCES=2 in a single container, or
start 2+ containers/replicas at the same time. 3. Observe: one instance acquires the licence lock and starts; the others crash during LicenseManager.initialize with unable to achieve a quorum during its retry window and exit.
It reproduces most reliably on first activation (longest lock hold), and intermittently on subsequent boots (refresh path). Also happens with rolling deployments with multiple instances/tasks registering simultaneously for a license. ### Expected Behaviour Concurrent boots should not crash. Suggested directions (any one would resolve it): Don't hold the distributed lock across the external licence-server HTTP call — do the network request outside the lock, or shrink the critical section to the DB read/write only.
Make the Redlock retry window / lock duration configurable (env), and/or raise the defaults so a waiting instance blocks instead of failing.
Treat lock-acquisition failure in LicenseManager.initialize as non-fatal: log, back off, and retry rather than letting the rejection propagate and exit the process. ### Current Workarounds Run a single Directus worker per container (PM2_INSTANCES=1).
Serialize instance startup so only one boots at a time (e.g. ECS maximumPercent that rolls one task at a time; deploy a single replica first, then scale up).
These avoid the contention but defeat horizontal/worker scaling during boot. ### Directus Version v12.0.2 ### Hosting Strategy Self-Hosted (Docker Image) ### Database Aurora MySQL 8
